title: Water, Hydrogen Bonding, and the Elements of Life
subject: AP Biology

chunks.text: A water molecule consists of two hydrogen atoms covalently bonded to one oxygen atom. Oxygen is much more electronegative than hydrogen, so it pulls the shared electrons toward itself, giving oxygen a partial negative charge and each hydrogen a partial positive charge.
Water is a polar molecule, meaning it has a partially negative region (the oxygen end) and partially positive regions (the hydrogen ends), even though the molecule is electrically neutral overall.

A hydrogen bond is an attraction between the partially positive hydrogen of one polar molecule and the partially negative atom of another. In water, hydrogen bonds form between the hydrogen of one molecule and the oxygen of a neighboring molecule.

A single hydrogen bond is weak, roughly twenty times weaker than the covalent bond within a water molecule. However, the enormous number of hydrogen bonds present in liquid water gives water its collective strength and life-supporting properties.

The covalent bonds that hold the hydrogen and oxygen atoms together inside a single water molecule are different from the hydrogen bonds that form between separate water molecules. Covalent bonds are intramolecular; hydrogen bonds are intermolecular.
Cohesion is the attraction of water molecules to other water molecules through hydrogen bonding. Cohesion allows water to form continuous columns and resist being pulled apart.

Adhesion is the attraction of water molecules to other polar surfaces, such as the glass walls of a tube or the cellulose walls of plant xylem. Adhesion helps water cling to surfaces and resist sliding back down.
Capillary action is the movement of water upward through a narrow space against gravity, produced by the combination of cohesion and adhesion.

In tall trees, water rises from roots to leaves through xylem without any pump. Transpiration (evaporation of water from leaves) creates tension that pulls a continuous, cohesive column of water upward, while adhesion holds the column to the xylem walls.

Surface tension is the tendency of a water surface to resist disruption. It arises because water molecules at the surface hydrogen-bond more tightly to the molecules beside and below them, forming a strong surface film that can support small insects or a floating needle.

Specific heat is the amount of energy required to raise the temperature of 1 gram of a substance by 1 degree Celsius. The specific heat of water is 4.18 J/(g·°C), which is exceptionally high compared with most substances.

Water resists temperature change because incoming heat energy must first break hydrogen bonds between molecules before the molecules can move faster. Since temperature measures molecular motion, energy spent breaking bonds does not immediately raise the temperature.

Water's high specific heat buffers temperature for living organisms, which are largely composed of water, and moderates the climate of oceans and coastal regions by absorbing heat during the day and releasing it slowly at night.

Water has a high heat of vaporization because many hydrogen bonds must be broken for water to evaporate. This makes evaporative cooling, such as sweating in animals and transpiration in plants, an efficient way to remove heat.

Water is called the universal solvent because its polarity lets it surround and separate charged or polar particles. Hydration occurs when water molecules surround ions, with negative oxygen ends facing positive ions and positive hydrogen ends facing negative ions.

Hydrophilic substances are polar or charged and dissolve readily in water; examples include salts, sugars, and amino acids. Hydrophobic substances are nonpolar and do not dissolve in water; examples include oils and fats.

Ice is about 9 percent less dense than liquid water because, as water cools below 4°C, hydrogen bonds lock the molecules into an open crystalline lattice that holds them farther apart than in liquid water. This is why ice floats.

Because ice floats, lakes and ponds freeze from the top down. The surface ice insulates the liquid water beneath, which stays near 4°C and allows fish, amphibians, and microorganisms to survive the winter.

Floating sea ice reflects sunlight back into space, an effect called albedo that helps regulate global temperature. When ice melts, the darker ocean surface absorbs more heat, creating a warming feedback loop important in climate science.
The six most abundant elements in living organisms are carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, and sulfur, often abbreviated CHNOPS.

Carbon is the backbone element of biological molecules because it has four valence electrons and can form four stable covalent bonds, allowing it to build long chains, branches, and rings and to bond with many other elements. Molecules built on carbon skeletons are called organic molecules.

Functional groups are specific clusters of atoms attached to a carbon skeleton that give a molecule characteristic chemical properties. The same functional group behaves the same way regardless of which molecule it is attached to.

Key functional groups in biology include the hydroxyl group (−OH, polar and water-soluble), the carboxyl group (−COOH, acidic, donates H⁺), the amino group (−NH₂, basic, accepts H⁺), the phosphate group (−PO₄, negatively charged and energy-carrying), the sulfhydryl group (−SH, forms disulfide bridges), and the methyl group (−CH₃, nonpolar).

A hydrocarbon, a molecule of only carbon and hydrogen, is nonpolar and mainly stores energy. Attaching polar functional groups such as hydroxyl groups makes a molecule more hydrophilic and more soluble in water.

On AP Biology free-response questions about water, full credit usually requires linking three things: the property (such as high specific heat), its molecular cause (polarity and hydrogen bonding), and a biological consequence (such as temperature buffering in organisms).
